title: Well proclaimed
hookLine: a teaching well proclaimed survives its teacher's death
tomorrow: The marks of a great man
last: HERE IS WHY I TRUST IT.

lines: ANANDA: TAKE THIS TO THE TEACHER.
cards: A young novice named Cunda has spent the rainy season near the town of Pava, and he has watched something unravel there.
A well-known teacher of the time, Nigantha Nataputta, has died, and his followers have split into camps, each telling the other it has the teaching wrong.
When the rains end, Cunda walks to Samagama, where Ananda is staying, and tells him everything. Ananda doesn't pass the story along.
He thinks of his own community and says: friend Cunda, this is worth bringing to the Blessed One. Let's go and tell him.

teach.b: Nigantha Nataputta is the teacher the Jain tradition honors as Mahavira, and Jains tell of his passing in their own texts and their own way.

The Pasadika Sutta, the pleasing discourse, uses the news only as a starting point and turns to the Buddha's own followers. What keeps a teaching alive after its teacher dies? The Buddha's answer has two parts.
First, it has to be well proclaimed: clearly taught, complete, its meaning made plain, so students aren't left guessing. Second, the students have to keep it that way. So he gives them a job.
Come together, all of you, and recite what I have taught, comparing meaning with meaning and wording with wording, so this holy life may last long, for the welfare of many.
And if a fellow student recites a teaching and the wording or the meaning seems off, don't applaud and don't scorn.
Ask, gently: friend, which fits better, this wording or that? This meaning or that? Keep asking until it's clear.

It's the habit of the four great references from a couple of weeks ago, now practiced together, out loud, kindly. And it's why the discourses still exist. For centuries they weren't written down at all.
People carried them by sitting together, reciting, checking each other, and keeping the words clear.
A teaching well proclaimed, held by students who keep proclaiming it well.

how: Buddhist monastics in many traditions still memorize and chant the discourses together, and the great councils of the tradition, from the first after the Buddha's death to modern ones, were recitations checked in common.

o: announced loudly to as many people as possible
taught clearly and completely, its meaning plain
declared official by a council of elders

p: the novice who brought the news
meaning with meaning, wording with wording
how to correct a fellow student

s: the Buddha tells the monks to argue down anyone who recites wrongly
he says neither applaud nor scorn; ask gently which wording and meaning fit better.
the discourses were carried for centuries by memory and recitation

games.q: you're Ananda. a novice brings news that a well-known teacher has died and his followers are quarreling. what do you do?
o: spread the news around the monastery.
take it to the Buddha, thinking of your own community's future.
ignore it: it's not your concern.
games.why: Ananda says it's worth bringing to the Blessed One, and the Buddha teaches how a teaching stays whole: recite it together.

practice: Choose one teaching you care about, from this path or anywhere, and say it to yourself in one clear sentence. Ask the sutta's gentle question, is this the right wording, the right meaning, then adjust it and say it again.
Let it rest clear in the background as you sit with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Well proclaimed. In DN 29 the Buddha says a clearly taught teaching, kept clear by students reciting together, survives its teacher. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali svakkhata: well proclaimed. the first word of the classic praise of the Dhamma.

carryVoice: Your line: ask gently, which fits better. A clear teaching, kept clear by friends. Day five hundred sixty-three, done.
